How do you feel about using "zones" for combat? I've always ran games either counting squares, or completely ignoring distance. In a theater-of-the-mind setting, squares doesn't work well, and completely ignoring distance slows down combat because players have ask about positions and relative distance. I was looking for better ways, to adjudicate, and found the zone thing. I've seen it in other games, but never D&D. It seems like it could work very well. It's assumed that you can move anywhere in your zone, move to an adjacent zone, and range attack into any zone. AoE attacks are a set number ahead of time. Has anyone run or played in games using zones? Any thoughts one way or the other?

I had a choose-your-own-adventure idea about the weekly themes. Each week the main event would have an obvious fail/succeed condition. This would affect the week directly after. I'm thinking the main faction of each borough will be greatly influenced by the outcome. 
For example
Week 1, all factions are vying for power, and the players will influence which two factions emerge as the economic or political powerhouse. 
Week 2, the two main factions wage espionage wars with each other, and players influence which emerges victorious.
Week 3, one factions is on top, and "the villain" is running this faction. At the end of week three, if the villain is defeated, the faction commits to independence. If players fail to defeat the villain, the faction joins the redcoats. 
Week 4, Players must try to gather more support for the war effort since the revolution is on now. This affects the whether the revolution or redcoats controls Fort Washington.
Week 5, no real decisions to make. Ft Washington is saved or not. The rebellion succeeds, or not.

These decisions should affect every part of the world. Including stock values of various companies, access to certain types of airships, weapons, allies. Players may have to turn against their boroughs. Others may become their local leaders.

What if trains are huge constructs that travel over land between cities. They are ancient magical constructs who are always on time. Companies have been able to attach cars to the train engines, and detach them at their destinations, but they can not control them in any way. The engines seem immune to any damage, but the cars are not. If cars are detached, and another train comes by, it will obliterate the cargo. The challenge will be to hitch a ride on the trains, but you cannot steer them. They will do what they do on a perfectly predictable schedule. The conflict comes in when you have to fight for the right to use the train at the station. Or when it’s known that two trains will be travelling side by side for a time, or maybe passing in opposite directions. They have ground deep “tracks” in the country side. Cities and boroughs have been built around them. Maybe they travel along the ley lines, and stop at conjunctions. If you have a personal train, it means that you have one or more cars that can latch onto the train and then will go to wherever you need. There is a schedule of train times. Some come every hour, some come once or twice a day. And some come only rarely. Say once per campaign.

so what happens if you apply Sovereign Glue to the tracks, wheels, axels, or some other moving part of the engine?

For sovereign glue, it takes one minute to cure. Besides that, if you are trying to glue an unstoppable force to an immovable object, I say, the train wins. I picture the engine more as a solid construct of force than an actual train engine.

But, maybe, for the determined player, if you glue things to it while it's stopped at a station, those things just get dragged around. Maybe the outside is littered with glued bodies of people who crossed the thieves guild. I think for this to work as truly indestructible, you would not have a track, just a trench gouged out by eons of train passing.

so a thought, but why not make a small table based on type (maybe 6 minor, 3 medium, 1 major possibilities might work so a d10, or move it to a % and have a ton of options) for every creature type.  Fiends table, humanoids table, undead, so forth.  then you have a number of rolls based on creature CR.  People with appropriate tool skills (tanning or cooking for instance) can have an extra roll if a dm says its appropriate

then you wouldn't need a full creature by creature rundown, instead just type by type.  Give subbosses and bosses specific bonus loot, possibly one of a kind stuff, or even the first of its kind (you could make tables get better each week, so for instance, dragon tooth might only become available after week 2, and the week 2 boss is the first drop of it guaranteed)

it keeps much of the flavor your aiming for, with only a fraction of the work, and is mechanics us video game nerds are used to.  in fact, slip in a bards tale like joke about loot (<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RZl9KcSywos>) and you even have a handwave for something odd dropping from a critter (how did the tarrasque drop chitin... cause video game mechanics)
